lead: Residential wiring carries electric power from the supply authority's service entrance to every lamp, socket, geyser and air conditioner in a home. Three wires run together: live at about 230 V, neutral at near earth potential, and earth for protection. The meter records energy, a main switch isolates the house, a distribution board splits the load into sub-circuits, and each sub-circuit has a fuse or miniature circuit breaker (MCB). A residual current circuit breaker (RCCB) watches for current leaking to earth. The purpose is simple: keep wires from overheating and keep people from shock.
prereq: You need: Ohm's law and power from Unit 1, DC Circuits and Network Theorems; Chapter 6.6 for load and bill; Chapter 6.2 for the energy meter.

blocks.text: The service entrance is where the utility's cable meets the building. It brings live (also called phase or line), neutral and protective earth. Live and neutral pass through the energy meter, which counts kilowatt-hours (kWh) for billing; see Chapter 6.2. Next is the main switch, a two-pole switch that disconnects both live and neutral so the board can be worked on safely. The supply then reaches the distribution board, where an RCCB sits first and a row of MCBs follows. Each MCB feeds one sub-circuit: lights and fans, 5 A sockets, a 16 A socket for a geyser or air conditioner.

items: Identify each sub-circuit and add the wattage of every appliance on it.
Apply a diversity factor D, because not all appliances run together; D is often 0.5 to 0.8 for homes.
Find design current I_b = (D × ΣP) / V, with ΣP in watts and V = 230 V.
Choose cable whose current capacity I_z is at least I_b.
Choose MCB rating I_n so that I_b ≤ I_n ≤ I_z.
Wire colour code: live brown or red, neutral blue or black, earth green or yellow-green. Older installations may use red live, black neutral and green earth.
A light circuit is wired with 1.0 or 1.5 mm² copper and a 5 A or 6 A MCB. A 16 A power circuit uses thicker copper.
The earth wire goes to every socket and metal body. It must never pass through a fuse or a switch.

sections.h3: Fuse and MCB: protecting the wiring

blocks.text: A fuse is a thin wire or strip that melts when current exceeds its rating. The rewirable fuse has a porcelain holder and a replaceable wire; it is cheap but slow and can be miswired. An HRC (high rupturing capacity) fuse has a ceramic body filled with sand and a silver element; it clears a short circuit in a few milliseconds without flame. Both protect the cable from overheating. They do not protect a person from shock.

An MCB (miniature circuit breaker) does the same job and resets. It has two trips. A bimetallic strip bends slowly on overload and trips after seconds or minutes. A magnetic coil trips instantly on a large short-circuit current. Standard ratings are 6, 10, 16, 20, 25 and 32 A. Type B, C and D curves set the instantaneous trip level.

blocks.where: I is current in amperes (A), P is power in watts (W), and V is supply voltage in volts (V), taken as 230 V for a single-phase home.
I_n is the nominal MCB rating in amperes and the 1.25 factor gives a 25 % margin for continuous load. Also I_n ≤ I_z, the cable current capacity.

blocks.text: An RCCB (residual current circuit breaker) compares the current in live and neutral. In a healthy circuit the two currents are equal, so their difference is zero. If a person touches live, some current flows through the body to earth and returns through the soil, not through the neutral. The difference, called residual current, operates a small current transformer and trips the breaker. A 30 mA RCCB is used for human protection; 100 mA or 300 mA units protect against fire. Some syllabi call this device an RCD (residual current device); an ELCB (earth leakage circuit breaker) is the older name.

An RCCB does not detect overload or a live-to-neutral short circuit, because those currents still return through neutral and cancel. It must be used with an MCB or fuse. Safety measures in a home include insulated conductors, closed boxes, earthing of metal bodies (see Chapter 6.8), a main switch that can be locked off, and never putting the earth wire through a fuse or switch. Before touching a circuit, switch off and test.

figure.caption: Power enters at the service, passes through the energy meter and main switch, then the RCCB, and the MCB board splits it into a 5 A light circuit and a 16 A power circuit. The RCCB is the only device that reacts to current leaking to earth.

spec.title: Residential distribution board
spec.aria: Service enters through an energy meter and main switch to an RCCB, then an MCB board splits into light and power circuits.

examples.question: A 230 V residential circuit supplies a 2 kW geyser. Find the current. Choose a standard MCB rating at least 25 % above the current from 6 A, 10 A, 16 A and 20 A.
steps: Given P = 2 kW = 2000 W and V = 230 V.
Current I = P / V = 2000 / 230 = 8.6957 A, which rounds to 8.70 A.
The standard ratings given are 6 A, 10 A, 16 A and 20 A. 10 A is below 10.87 A, so the next size up is 16 A.
Check cable capacity: the 16 A MCB needs a cable rated at least 16 A, for example 2.5 mm² copper.
examples.answer: The geyser draws 8.70 A, and the chosen MCB rating is 16 A.
examples.check:
P = 2000
V = 230
I = P / V
req = 1.25 * I
ratings = [6, 10, 16, 20]
chosen = [r for r in ratings if r >= req][0]
print(f"{I:.2f}")
print(f"{req:.2f}")
print(chosen)

traps: A fuse or MCB protects the wiring, not people. The RCCB protects people. An answer that says 'the MCB prevents shock' loses marks.
Never put the earth wire through a fuse or a switch. An open earth makes the metal body live.
An RCCB is not an overload device. It does not replace an MCB, and an MCB does not replace an RCCB.
2 kW is 2000 W, not 2 W. At 230 V the current is about 8.7 A, not 0.87 A.
Old and new wire colours differ. Read the question's code before labelling live and neutral.

quiz.q: Which conductor is connected to the metal body of an appliance, and what colour is it?
quiz.a: The protective earth conductor; green or yellow-green.

quiz.q: Name two standard MCB current ratings.
quiz.a: 6 A and 16 A (also 10 A, 20 A, 25 A, 32 A).

quiz.q: Why does an RCCB not trip on an overload?
quiz.a: In an overload the extra current returns through neutral, so live and neutral currents remain equal; residual current is zero. An MCB or fuse must clear overload.

quiz.q: A 1500 W heater runs at 230 V. Find the current and choose an MCB from 6 A, 10 A, 16 A with a 25 % margin.
A home has 8 lamps of 60 W, 6 fans of 75 W, one 2 kW geyser and one 1.5 kW AC. Take diversity 0.6. Find design current and a suitable MCB from 6, 10, 16, 20, 25 A.
Why is the earth wire never taken through a fuse or a switch?
quiz.a: If the earth path opens, a fault makes the metal body live and no fault current flows, so the MCB or RCCB may not trip. The earth must stay continuous.

quiz.q: State one difference between a fuse and an MCB.
quiz.a: A fuse melts and must be replaced; an MCB trips and can be reset.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern homes add RCBOs, which combine an MCB and an RCCB in one module, and surge protection devices (SPDs) for lightning and switching spikes. Smart energy meters and home automation boards report circuit-level consumption and can trip remotely. Indian standards for wiring installations are published by the Bureau of Indian Standards; search for IS 732 and the National Electrical Code. Arc fault detection devices (AFDDs) are appearing in newer codes to catch loose connections that start fires.
